section_title: What will make the restored worship different?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 39 And as for you, O house of Israel, this is what the Lord GOD says: Go and serve your idols, every one of you. But afterward, you will surely listen to Me, and you will no longer defile My holy name with your gifts and idols. 40 For on My holy mountain, the high mountain of Israel, declares the Lord GOD, there the whole house of Israel, all of them, will serve Me in the land. There I will accept them and will require your offerings and choice gifts, along with all your holy sacrifices. 41 When I bring you from the peoples and gather you from the lands to which you have been scattered, I will accept you as a pleasing aroma. And I will show My holiness through you in the sight of the nations.

42 Then you will know that I am the LORD, when I bring you into the land of Israel, the land that I swore to give your fathers. 43 There you will remember your ways and all the deeds with which you have defiled yourselves, and you will loathe yourselves for all the evils you have done. 44 Then you will know, O house of Israel, that I am the LORD, when I have dealt with you for the sake of My name and not according to your wicked ways and corrupt acts, declares the Lord GOD.”

context_lines: The Lord’s challenge to serve the idols is followed by a promise that this divided worship will not continue. His name will no longer be profaned by gifts offered alongside idolatry.
The whole house of Israel will serve Him on His holy mountain. He will accept the people and their offerings when He gathers them, showing His holiness through them in the sight of the nations.
The people will know Him as the Lord who brings them to the land promised to their fathers. They will remember and recoil from the ways in which they defiled themselves.

The ending explains why their restoration is possible: He deals with them for His name’s sake, rather than according to their wicked conduct. Accepted worship and repentance grow out of His merciful action.
common_interpretation_lines: [Wesley](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/ezekiel/20.htm) connects the promise with restored worship in Jerusalem and the people’s sorrow over their former ways. [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/ezekiel/20.htm) likewise emphasizes repentance produced through God’s kindness and a fuller recognition of His holiness.

The promise is more than the recovery of prosperity. The people’s relation to the Lord and their judgment of their own former conduct have changed. Their future gives the nations a reason to recognize His holiness, rather than to associate His name with their idols.
god_plan_lines: [Revelation 7:9–17](https://biblehub.com/bsb/revelation/7.htm) presents a multitude from every nation worshiping God and the Lamb. Their robes have been washed in the Lamb’s blood, they serve before God, and the Lamb shepherds them to living water.

Revelation does not explicitly identify that multitude with the whole house of Israel in Ezekiel 20. The shared theme is a people gathered and accepted for worship through God’s saving provision. Revelation develops the wider hope through the Lamb and brings the nations into the picture of life in God’s presence.
